title: The hypertrophy series: stimulus to fatigue ratio
summary: NH argues the popular stimulus-to-fatigue ratio debate is mostly empty because both terms are too vague, and that fatigue must be broken down into types (muscular, cardiovascular, mechanical, tendon, CNS). He proposes a push-up test to gauge whether a session caused enough muscular damage and defends the deadlift's high fatigue as an efficient way to rack up tonnage. For bodybuilders, controlled fatigue is a good thing.
claims: The stimulus-to-fatigue ratio debate is mostly unproductive because 'stimulus' and 'fatigue' are too loosely defined to support a sensible argument
Fatigue has to be specified: it can be muscular, cardiovascular, mechanical, tendon or CNS fatigue, each with its own sub-types
Doing 10x10 with a non-challenging weight or 30 reps at about 40% of max builds lots of fatigue, but mostly cardiovascular rather than the muscular fatigue that damages fibers
Most people should not worry about accumulating too much muscular fatigue; only very motivated novices prone to overdoing it and getting hurt should heed that advice
You will know a muscle is no longer fit to be worked because you simply cannot use it anymore

Push-up test: if your baseline is 30 push-ups and after a bench workout you still get 30 then 29, the bench session did not damage the fibers enough; dropping to 20 on the second set shows a growth-producing stimulus
Like tonnage, stimulus comes in quality and junk forms; merely 'stimulating' a muscle is not enough for hypertrophy
A load you cannot complete, like a squat you cannot stand up, is a stimulus that exceeded your ability and is therefore too high
How much session volume you can recover from is individual, not an exact science, and fully testable on yourself
The more interesting stimulus-to-fatigue question is at the level of individual lifts, e.g. claims that some lifts cause too much fatigue to be worth it
Anyone in shape should be able to deadlift, even for high reps, without getting gassed; cardiovascular endurance should match muscular endurance
He does not encourage high-rep deadlifts, for other reasons than cardio
The deadlift fatigues most people through tendon and mechanical fatigue because they cannot maintain thoracic extension, not because it is a bad lift
Because the deadlift hits so many muscles with maximal loads, it spreads damage widely and racks up large tonnage in little time, saving work later in the session

When you know the type of fatigue you are getting and control volume and intensity, fatigue becomes neutral; for bodybuilders it is usually good and the goal is the maximum fatigue you can recover from
Fatigue is created by stimulus and there is no stimulus without fatigue; if you are not fatigued you did not push enough to grow
exercises: sets to failure after bench to compare against baseline
diagnostic of how much damage the bench session did
time-efficient full-body tonnage; fatigue mostly tendon/mechanical when form fails
